text: This chapter builds one real deliverable across four lessons: a small, genuinely production-quality quantum software library, applying every practice from the previous five chapters. This lesson scopes it and writes the requirements before any code gets written.

This lesson covers scoping a capstone library so it's achievable in a few lessons but still demonstrates every chapter's practices, writing a requirements document that references earlier lessons as acceptance criteria, choosing algorithms based on what best exercises each technique, and setting up the project skeleton before any algorithm code exists.

The capstone library, called quantumlib, implements three well-understood algorithms, deliberately not novel research, since the point is demonstrating software-engineering discipline, not algorithmic originality. Bell pair and GHZ state preparation exercises construction tests and the statevector debugging technique with minimal circuit complexity. Grover's search at three to four qubits exercises statistical testing meaningfully and the iteration-count resource-estimation formula. A small QAOA instance exercises the backend-abstraction pattern and the shot-budget estimation work, since it's the one genuinely iterative, hybrid algorithm in the set.

A requirements document for this capstone states, for each algorithm, concrete acceptance criteria tied directly to specific chapter content — construction separated from execution, construction tests parametrized across qubit counts, a statevector test confirming exact structure, a statistical test with an explicit confidence level. Each line is checkable — a reviewer can look at the code and confirm it either does or doesn't satisfy that specific, lesson-referenced requirement, rather than arguing about what 'well-tested' means in the abstract.

Apply the project-structure lesson's layout immediately, before writing a single circuit: a pinned pyproject.toml, a README stating scope and SDK versions, and src folders for circuits, backends, analysis, and estimation, plus a tests folder. Lesson 22 fills in the circuits, backends, and matching tests. Lesson 23 fills in documentation. Lesson 24 is the final review.

Explicitly, before starting: done means every requirement in that document is satisfied and verifiably checkable, the full tiered test suite passes, dependencies are pinned with a committed lockfile, and the README documents validated backends. It does not mean the algorithms produced correct answers once in a demo — that bar was explicitly rejected back in lesson one. Next lesson writes the actual code for all three modules, for real.
